cards.front: An {{c1::ecosystem}} is all the living things in a place together with their nonliving surroundings.
cards.quote: An ecosystem is all the living things in a place together with their nonliving surroundings.
cards.section: Read an ecosystem in two parts

cards.front: What is a biotic factor in an ecosystem? Give an example of an interaction.
cards.back: A living part: plants, animals, fungi and microorganisms, and the ways they interact, such as a deer eating acorns.
cards.quote: A biotic factor is a living part: plants, animals, fungi and microorganisms, and the ways they interact, such as a deer eating acorns.
cards.section: Read an ecosystem in two parts

cards.front: What is an abiotic factor? Name the important examples.
cards.back: A nonliving part. Examples: climate, sunlight, water, soil, air and nutrients.
cards.quote: An abiotic factor is a nonliving part. Important examples are climate, sunlight, water, soil, air and nutrients.
cards.section: Read an ecosystem in two parts

cards.front: A soil sample contains sand, clay, minerals, worms, fungi and bacteria. Is the whole sample biotic or abiotic?
cards.back: It is mixed. The sand, clay and minerals are abiotic. The worms, fungi and bacteria living in it are biotic.
cards.quote: The sand, clay and minerals are abiotic. The worms, fungi and bacteria living in it are biotic.
cards.section: Read an ecosystem in two parts

cards.front: {{c1::Climate}} is the usual pattern of temperature and precipitation (rain and snow) in a place over many years.
cards.quote: climate, the usual pattern of temperature and precipitation (rain and snow) in a place over many years
cards.section: Climate is a long-term abiotic condition

cards.front: What is the main reason Virginia has hot summers and cold winters?
cards.back: Earth's tilt as it travels around the sun, not Earth's changing distance from the sun.
cards.why: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees.
cards.quote: That tilt, not Earth's changing distance from the sun, is the main reason Virginia has hot summers and cold winters.
cards.section: Climate is a long-term abiotic condition

cards.front: Two Virginia sites are measured on the same summer day. One is on a high mountaintop and the other is on the coast. Which is usually cooler, and why?
cards.back: The mountaintop is usually cooler, because air usually cools as elevation rises. Being slightly closer to the sun does not make it warmer.
cards.quote: The high mountaintop is usually cooler, because air usually cools as elevation rises.
cards.section: Climate is a long-term abiotic condition

cards.front: What is topography, and how can it change the climate from one side of a mountain to the other?
cards.back: Topography is the shape of the land. It can make one side of a mountain wet and the far side dry.
cards.quote: Topography, the shape of the land, can make one side of a mountain wet and the far side dry.
cards.section: Climate is a long-term abiotic condition

cards.front: How do people change climate? Name the gas and what it does.
cards.back: Burning fossil fuels adds carbon dioxide to the air. It is a nonliving gas that traps heat.
cards.quote: Burning fossil fuels adds carbon dioxide, a nonliving gas that traps heat, to the air.
cards.section: Climate is a long-term abiotic condition

cards.front: Why do ecosystems change over time?
cards.back: Climate, population sizes and the kinds of species all change over time, so ecosystems change too.
cards.quote: Climate, population sizes and the kinds of species all change over time, so ecosystems change too.
cards.section: Climate is a long-term abiotic condition

cards.front: Dead parts and wastes of living things: does the lesson count them as biotic or abiotic?
cards.back: They are often counted as biotic, even though they are no longer alive. Soil is the other case that blurs the line.
cards.quote: Dead parts and wastes of living things are often counted as biotic, as you saw in Food Webs and Energy.
cards.section: Read an ecosystem in two parts

cards.front: {{c1::Salinity}} is the amount of salt dissolved in water.
cards.quote: Salinity is the amount of salt dissolved in water.
cards.section: Compare land, fresh water and salt water

cards.front: What is an estuary, and how does its salinity behave?
cards.back: A mixing zone where fresh river water meets salty ocean water, such as the Chesapeake Bay. Its salinity is in between and shifts with rain and season.
cards.quote: Its salinity is in between, and it shifts with rain and season.
cards.section: Compare land, fresh water and salt water

cards.front: Salt is the sharpest difference between freshwater and marine ecosystems. About how much salt does each have, in parts per thousand?
cards.back: Freshwater: under about 0.5. Open ocean: about 35.
cards.quote: Salt is the sharpest difference in the table, from under 0.5 to about 35 parts per thousand.
cards.section: Compare land, fresh water and salt water

cards.front: In Chesapeake Bay data, what does a salinity of 1 PSU mean?
cards.back: About 1 gram of salt in 1,000 grams of water.
cards.quote: In Bay data, 1 PSU is about the same as 1 gram of salt in 1,000 grams of water.
cards.section: Use salinity data from the James

cards.front: Mean summer salinity was 20.67 PSU at LE5.4 and 0.09 PSU at TF5.5. How much saltier is LE5.4? Is the difference closer to 2 or 20 PSU?
cards.back: Subtract: 20.67 - 0.09 = 20.58 PSU, close to 20 PSU. Adding would answer a different question.
cards.quote: Subtract: 20.67 − 0.09 = 20.58 PSU, close to 20 PSU.
cards.section: Use salinity data from the James

cards.front: A guide says salinity from 10 to 28 is good for eastern oysters, and oysters can die if it stays below 5 for a long time. Stations along the James have mean summer salinities of 0.09, 1.32, 4.53, 11.54, 15.39, 20.67, 23.06 and 25.78 PSU. Which are in the good range, and which are below 5?
cards.back: Good range: 11.54 through 25.78 PSU (stations LE5.2 through CB7.4). Below 5: 0.09, 1.32 and 4.53 PSU (TF5.5, RET5.2 and LE5.1).
cards.quote: Good range: LE5.2 through CB7.4 (11.54 to 25.78 PSU).
cards.section: Use salinity data from the James

cards.front: A station's mean summer salinity is below 5 PSU. Does that alone show that oysters would die there?
cards.back: No. A summer mean does not show that the water stays that low for a long time, and oysters die only if it stays very low for a long time.
cards.quote: A summer mean alone does not show that the water stays that low for a long time.
cards.section: Use salinity data from the James

cards.front: The salinity table lists eelgrass as an example for station CB7.4. Does that show eelgrass was growing there?
cards.back: No. The column shows possible habitat. Nobody counted these organisms at the stations, and the ranges overlap.
cards.quote: Nobody counted these organisms at the stations, and the ranges overlap.
cards.section: Use salinity data from the James

cards.front: In a brine shrimp hatching test where salt is the only condition changed (0, 10, 20, 30 and 40 grams per liter), which cup is the control, and what does it show?
cards.back: The cup with no salt. It shows what happens in fresh water.
cards.quote: Control: the cup with no salt shows what happens in fresh water.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the brine shrimp test, what are the independent and dependent variables?
cards.back: Independent: salt per liter of water. Dependent: the number of hatched shrimp counted in a 1-milliliter sample after 48 hours.
cards.quote: Independent variable: salt per liter of water: 0, 10, 20, 30 and 40 grams.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the brine shrimp test, why use three cups at each salt level and find the mean?
cards.back: Three cups at each level give repeated trials, and the mean for each level is what you compare.
cards.quote: Trials: three cups at each salt level. Find the mean for each level.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A site on the James has salinity in the good range for oysters, but no oyster reef grows there. Give two reasons this can happen, using the lesson's rule.
cards.back: (1) No factor acts alone, so other conditions limit survival; (2) living interactions such as predators also help decide where reefs grow.
cards.quote: Living interactions such as predators also help decide where reefs grow.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking

cards.front: Brine shrimp hatching changes a lot between salt levels in cups. What can you conclude, and what can you not conclude about where they live in the wild?
cards.back: Salinity affects this one stage of the brine shrimp life cycle. A cup is a model, not a real salt lake, so it does not show where shrimp live in the wild.
cards.quote: If hatching changes a lot from one salt level to another, salinity affects this one stage of the brine shrimp life cycle.
cards.section: Design problem
